questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish new social movements from traditional class-based organisations
questions.stem: Log, 3 November, seeing excellent: from the ridge I watched neighbours who had never joined a union organise over hospital closures.

options.text: They illustrate new social movements, which organise around identity, quality of life and post-material concerns
They illustrate a traditional labour movement, because public service campaigns depend on wage-based class solidarity
options.misconception: assumes any service campaign is traditional class politics

options.text: They illustrate a single-issue pressure group, since identity claims carry no long-term organisational structure
options.misconception: reads every campaign as a narrow pressure group

options.text: They illustrate an established party, because residents had already registered with a national organisation
options.misconception: assumes residents belonged to a formal party

questions.explanation: New social movements organise around identity and post-material goals rather than class and wages. The log shows residents rallying over values, not pay bargaining, which is the defining feature.
questions.hint: Focus on what the campaign was about, not who joined.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret bargaining leverage from a bargaining outcome
questions.stem: Clear horizon at dawn: the union had 1,200 members, the employer conceded two of three demands, and the delegate praised the offer.

options.text: The employer conceded because the union's membership had doubled overnight
options.misconception: assumes membership growth explains the concession

options.text: The union's leverage came from threatening a costly strike that few members wanted
The delegate's praise shows the union had abandoned its demands
options.misconception: reads praise as evidence of surrender

options.text: The employer conceded only because a rival union offered the same terms
options.misconception: invents a rival union not mentioned in the log

questions.explanation: Leverage is the capacity to make refusal costlier than concession. A credible but unwanted strike threat raises the cost of refusal, and praise for the offer shows satisfaction rather than surrender.
questions.hint: Ask what made refusal expensive for the employer.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Order the stages of a movement campaign
questions.stem: Hazy moonless night: I sketched the stages of the housing campaign, from the petition through the media coverage to the hearing.

answer.exemplar: A complete sequence runs from identifying a grievance, through mobilisation and agenda-setting with decision-makers, to media amplification and pressure at the point of decision. Each stage depends on the one before it, so skipping agenda-setting leaves the later stages without a target and little chance of uptake.

questions.explanation: Campaigns progress from grievance definition to mobilisation, agenda-setting, amplification and pressure at the decision point. Skipping a stage leaves later phases without a target and reduces the chance of uptake.
questions.hint: Order the stages from grievance to decision.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the effect of an electoral access reform on the register
questions.stem: Log, 12 June: the electorate numbered 6,400 before automatic registration, which added 1,500 newly registered voters. How many registered voters are there now?
questions.explanation: The reform adds the newly registered voters to the existing electorate, so 6,400 plus 1,500 equals 7,900 voters. Subtracting would wrongly treat registration as a replacement for existing names.
questions.hint: Add the new names to the existing electorate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the two-step flow to a campaign leaflet

stimulus.body: A neighbourhood flyer asks residents to sign a petition on hospital closures and names two local organisers. The organisers say they will pass the petition to the council on Friday.

questions.stem: Under the two-step model, how does this leaflet's route to the council fit the pattern?

options.text: Residents persuade local organisers, who then carry the issue to the council
Each resident contacts the council directly and the organisers merely print leaflets
options.misconception: assumes direct mass contact rather than opinion leaders

options.text: The council persuades the organisers, who then rally residents to sign
options.misconception: reverses the direction of influence

options.text: Opinion leaders read the leaflet alone and act without any resident contact
options.misconception: assumes opinion leaders act with no mass contact

questions.explanation: The two-step flow routes messages from the public to opinion leaders, who then pass them to decision-makers. The leaflet names organisers for exactly this relay role, so the campaign expects no mass direct lobbying.
questions.hint: Trace who contacts whom, in order.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a nomination outcome as evidence of gatekeeping
questions.stem: Steady seeing: the nomination panel interviewed 24 hopeful candidates and endorsed 9 of them for the ballot.

options.text: The endorsement rate of 37.5 per cent shows an unusually narrow gate
options.misconception: mislabels a 37.5 per cent rate as 62.5 per cent

options.text: Endorsing 9 of 24 means about 38 per cent of candidates cleared the gate
The panel endorsed 9 of 24, so a clear majority of hopefuls got the nomination
options.misconception: treats a minority endorsement as a majority

options.text: The panel interviewed 24, so about 15 candidates must have been rejected
options.misconception: misreads the denominator as the rejection count

questions.explanation: Nine out of twenty-four is 37.5 per cent, so roughly 38 per cent of candidates cleared the gate. Reading the panel's work as a majority endorsement reverses the ratio.
questions.hint: Divide nine by twenty-four.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain post-victory demobilisation in a movement context
questions.stem: Warm night, no dew: the campaign that had filled the square every Saturday suddenly met a crowd of a dozen people.

options.text: The movement collapsed because the city council reversed its decision overnight
options.misconception: attributes demobilisation to a single policy reversal

options.text: The campaign ended because the organisers moved on to a different, unrelated issue
options.misconception: reads issue succession as a second defeat

options.text: This is typical post-victory demobilisation, when routine is displaced by governing
The movement is dead because the square could not legally hold large gatherings
options.misconception: assumes legal bans explain every crowd drop

questions.explanation: Post-victory demobilisation is common because campaigns are built for opposition, not for the long administrative work of governing. A drop after a win is therefore routine, not evidence of a ban or a policy reversal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the goal was achieved or merely lost.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how participation reforms widen electoral access
questions.stem: Log entry under cloud: the town hall debated whether to move polling to the evening and to register students at their colleges.

answer.exemplar: Participation reforms widen access by removing practical barriers rather than by changing preferences. Evening polling suits shift workers, campus registration reaches students who never appear at the town hall, and postal voting helps those who cannot attend at all. Each measure lowers the cost of voting for a specific group of citizens.

questions.explanation: Participation reforms target practical barriers such as timing, distance and registration method. Evening polls, campus registration and postal voting each reduce the cost of voting for a distinct group of citizens.
questions.hint: Look for barriers removed, not opinions changed.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a turnout share from eligible and voting figures
questions.stem: Log, 20 March: the parish had 5,200 eligible voters and 2,340 of them cast a ballot. What percentage of the electorate voted?
questions.explanation: Two thousand three hundred forty divided by five thousand two hundred equals exactly 0.45, so turnout was 45 per cent. Using the eligible count rather than registered voters keeps the measure comparable.
questions.hint: Cast ballots divided by eligible voters.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a cohort effect in turnout data
questions.stem: Frost on the lens: the young who protested in the 1990s now voted in the highest turnout bracket of the 2020s.

options.text: Turnout rose because the campaign of the 2020s covered more issues
options.misconception: attributes cohort change to issue coverage

options.text: Turnout rose because the older generation finally became politically interested
options.misconception: confuses a cohort effect with a period effect

options.text: Turnout rose because young voters were granted a new voting right
options.misconception: assumes a franchise change caused the shift

options.text: This is a cohort effect, as the same age group carries its habits forward

questions.explanation: A cohort effect holds that the formative experiences of a generation persist as its members age. The same young cohort voting at high rates decades later suggests durable habits rather than a change in current conditions.
questions.hint: Separate age, period and cohort effects.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the organisational autonomy claimed by new social movements

options.text: It avoided those labels because its members had all left the traditional left
options.misconception: assumes rejection of the old left

options.text: It avoided those labels because it expected to contest the next election
options.misconception: confuses a pressure group with a party

options.text: It avoided those labels because new movements build identity around autonomy
It avoided those labels because it intended to merge with an existing party
options.misconception: assumes a planned merger with a party

questions.explanation: New social movements often reject the union and party labels to signal autonomy from established hierarchies. Identity-based organisation, not electoral ambition, explains the refusal to use those names.
questions.hint: Think about what the naming itself signals.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the source of bargaining leverage in a relationship
questions.stem: Clouds lifting: the tenants' group discovered that the landlord depended on the group staying organised.

options.text: Leverage comes from the number of tenants who attend the monthly meeting
options.misconception: confuses participation numbers with bargaining power

options.text: Leverage comes from the tenant group having registered as a formal company
options.misconception: assumes legal form creates bargaining power

options.text: Leverage comes from the landlord's dislike of the group's newsletter
options.misconception: reads a nuisance tactic as structural leverage

options.text: Leverage comes from the landlord's dependence on the group's continued unity

questions.explanation: Leverage rests on making refusal costly, here because the landlord needs the group intact to make concessions. Meeting numbers, legal form and irritation are not themselves sources of bargaining power.
questions.hint: Ask what the other side actually needs.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse a campaign that advances through agenda-setting rather than lobbying
questions.stem: Midnight, moon bright: I wrote down how the students' petition reached the council agenda without anyone lobbying directly.

answer.exemplar: The sequence worked through agenda-setting rather than direct lobbying: the petition gathered signatures, a sympathetic councillor tabled it, the council placed it on the agenda, and a hearing created the pressure point. Success depended on each step feeding the next, with the media stage amplifying the moment of the vote.

questions.explanation: The petition moved signatures, a councillor tabled it and the agenda stage supplied the pressure point. Media amplification came later, so the sequence did not rely on direct lobbying at all.
questions.hint: Find the stage that created the pressure point.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the two-step flow to an official message

options.text: The council reached the street directly through the noticeboard message
options.misconception: treats a posted notice as direct mass communication

options.text: Almost nobody saw it, so the council's message had no effect at all
options.misconception: assumes direct contact is the only route

options.text: Local opinion leaders carried the message onward to neighbours who missed it
The message spread through formal party channels rather than personal ones
options.misconception: confuses two-step flow with party communication

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of candidates who reach a party ballot
questions.stem: Log, 8 May: of the 40 people who asked the party for nomination, 10 were shortlisted and 4 won the contest.

options.text: The gate was wide open, since 10 of the 40 hopefuls were shortlisted
options.misconception: reads a shortlist of ten as a weak gate

options.text: Most of the field was eliminated, since 30 of the 40 never reached the shortlist
options.misconception: treats shortlisting as the same as winning

options.text: The gate produced 10 candidates for 4 places, so the contest itself was decisive
options.misconception: ignores how few applicants entered the gate

options.text: Only 4 of the 40 applicants, about 10 per cent, reached the final list

questions.explanation: Four of forty applicants is one in ten, so about 10 per cent of the field reached the ballot. Shortlisting is an intermediate stage, so counting the ten shortlisted people as the final gate overstates openness.
questions.hint: Count from the original forty downwards.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a movement's activity declines after it wins
questions.stem: Sky washed clean after rain: the housing movement won its campaign and the weekly rally was quietly cancelled.

options.text: Demobilisation is expected once the objective has been achieved
The cancellation proves the leaders had never wanted the housing outcome
options.misconception: infers bad faith from a routine cancellation

options.text: The cancellation shows the council had already agreed the deal in secret
options.misconception: invents a secret bargain to explain the end

options.text: The cancellation proves the movement's membership was dissolved by its leader
options.misconception: assumes a single leader dissolved the group

questions.explanation: Movements mobilise around a specific grievance and tend to lose energy once that grievance is resolved. Cancelling the rally after a win is the expected pattern, not evidence of hidden deals or bad faith.
questions.hint: Expect the routine pattern of a successful campaign.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an access reform by its effect on previously missing voters
questions.stem: Log, grey and damp: I compared the town's old polling station with the new one placed near the housing estate.

answer.exemplar: Reform should be judged by whether the change removed a barrier that had suppressed participation. Placing the polling station near the estate cuts the distance that older and less mobile residents had to travel, so the relevant question is not whether the venue looks better but how many of those previously missing residents now vote.

questions.explanation: Access reform works by removing practical barriers, so a relocated polling station should be judged by who it brings back to the vote. Counting the venue's appearance rather than the change in turnout misses the point.
questions.hint: Judge the reform by who returns to vote.

questions.explanation: Three hundred out of two thousand is 0.15, so participation among young residents was 15 per cent. Expressing it as a share of the resident population rather than of the invited group is what makes the figure meaningful.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a cohort effect from a period effect in turnout data

options.text: The persistent gap shows the electoral system systematically excludes younger voters
options.misconception: attributes a stable gap to system design

options.text: The persistent gap shows that the campaign issues of 1985 mattered most
options.misconception: explains a stable gap with old issue salience

options.text: The persistent gap is consistent with a cohort effect carried by each age group

options.misconception: equates a values campaign with party organisation

options.text: The employer reopened talks because a well-organised boycott threatened losses
The employer reopened talks to delay the settlement for a further year
options.misconception: assumes delay is always the employer's goal

options.text: The employer reopened talks because the law required a union ballot
options.misconception: assumes a legal duty to reopen negotiations

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a quiet mobilisation stage prepares a later peak

answer.exemplar: The stalls were the mobilisation stage: they identified what would and would not attract supporters and let organisers build a list of committed volunteers. questions.explanation: Early stalls served mobilisation, identifying willing supporters and building the reliable turnout that later made the hearing crowded. The quiet opening phase was groundwork, not failure.
questions.hint: Identify the purpose of the quiet early phase.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how media amplification fits into a campaign sequence
questions.stem: Log, 12 March: after the news covered the petition, the letters to the editor multiplied for a fortnight and then stopped.

answer.exemplar: The sequence ran from mobilisation through agenda-setting to media amplification and back into selective pressure. The press coverage enlarged the issue, correspondence peaked in the week that followed, and then the campaign moved to the decision stage, which is why new letters stopped while the real pressure began.

questions.explanation: Letters peaked after coverage because that was the amplification stage, then stopped as the campaign moved to the decision stage. Activity after the media peak is not decline but a change of tactic.
questions.hint: Match each burst of activity to a stage.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the register size after an enrolment reform
questions.stem: Log, 30 January: a city with 300,000 registered voters added 4,500 through a reform for citizens registered abroad. What is the new registered total?
questions.explanation: Adding the 4,500 newly registrable residents to 300,000 gives 304,500 registered voters. The figure is an addition because those citizens were previously outside the register entirely.
questions.hint: Add the overseas registrations to the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two-step pattern in a resident's account

stimulus.body: Asked why neighbours had signed the petition about the bus route, one resident said the local shopkeeper had explained it to her. The shopkeeper said he had read the council leaflet and thought it mattered.

questions.stem: Given this account, which description best matches the communication pattern?

options.text: The council leaflet reached every household directly by post
options.misconception: ignores the shopkeeper's relay role

options.text: The shopkeeper persuaded the council to change the bus route
options.misconception: reverses the direction of influence

options.text: The leaflet reached the shopkeeper, who then reached the neighbours
The neighbours found the leaflet themselves and informed the shopkeeper
options.misconception: inverts who informed whom

questions.explanation: The account traces information from the council leaflet to the shopkeeper and then to neighbours, which is the two-step flow. The resident did not read the leaflet and the shopkeeper did not approach the council.
questions.hint: Follow the information's path.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the number of candidates as a measure of gatekeeping
questions.stem: Log, 6 September: in a ward of 9,000 voters the party endorsed one candidate who received 1,800 votes.

options.text: One candidate for the whole ward shows tight control over who may stand
Only 20 per cent voted, so the ward was poorly organised
options.misconception: reads a single candidate as poor organisation

options.text: The candidate polled well, so the gatekeeping was clearly ineffective
options.misconception: confuses vote share with nomination control

options.text: The ward had 9,000 voters, so the party fielded about eight candidates
options.misconception: divides voters by votes to invent a candidate count

questions.explanation: Gatekeeping shows in the number of candidates a party allows to stand, and one endorsed candidate is tight control. Vote share and ward size say nothing about how nomination power was exercised.
questions.hint: Count candidates, not votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the shift from campaigning to administration
questions.stem: Log, 4 August: the group that had campaigned for six years now meets monthly, mainly to sign off minutes.

options.text: Monthly meetings prove the leadership has become bureaucratic and lazy
options.misconception: judges routine administration as incompetence

options.text: Monthly meetings show the campaign's goals were secretly abandoned
options.misconception: assumes an abandonment the log does not record

options.text: Monthly meetings show the group is waiting for the next election to begin
options.misconception: assumes an electoral pause drives the schedule

options.text: A routinised group with reduced activity is typical after a campaign's goal is met

questions.explanation: Once a campaign's demand is satisfied, the machinery built to fight it loses its function and activity drops sharply. Routine administration after the goal is met is the expected pattern, not a sign of laziness or betrayal.
questions.hint: Recall what campaigns are built to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain a participation reform targeting cost and distance barriers
questions.stem: Log, 21 November: the council debated whether to fund free transport for disabled voters to reach polling stations.

answer.exemplar: Funding transport targets a specific barrier that no rule about voting rights can remove, because distance and cost silently suppress the vote of those least able to travel. A measure like this should be assessed by whether disabled residents who were previously missing now vote, not by whether it appears in any statutory list of voting rights.

questions.explanation: Cost and distance suppress participation without any denial of formal rights, so funding transport addresses a real barrier. The test is whether previously missing disabled residents now vote.
questions.hint: Look for barriers that rules alone cannot remove.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the registered share of petition signatories
questions.stem: Log, 18 February: a petition attracted 900 signatures, of which 270 came from residents eligible to vote in the election. What percentage of signatories were registered voters?
questions.explanation: Two hundred seventy out of nine hundred equals 0.30, so 30 per cent of signatories were registered voters. This is the selection effect visible in a petition, where the electorate is only part of the population present.
questions.hint: Divide registered voters by all signatories.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a turnout gap using evidence across elections
questions.stem: Log, 25 October: turnout rose among voters over fifty and fell among voters under thirty, in the same year.

options.text: These are age effects, because turnout always differs between the two groups
options.misconception: collapses cohort and age into one thing

options.text: These are period effects, since the same year produced both changes
options.misconception: treats a shared year as the whole explanation

options.text: These are cohort effects, since the groups differ across every recent election
These are pure registration effects, since only registered voters can turn out
options.misconception: reduces turnout gaps to registration lists

questions.explanation: When the same age groups differ in every recent election, the pattern is cohort based, because habits formed long ago persist. A period explanation would require the gap to shift with events in the year.
questions.hint: Check whether the gap repeats each year.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the rejection of class labels in a values movement
questions.stem: Log, 15 December: the group organised around clean air and cycling, and its members rejected the label of class struggle.

options.text: Rejecting class labels fits new social movements organised around post-material values
Rejecting class labels shows the group had secretly adopted a rival class analysis
options.misconception: infers a hidden ideology from a public label

options.text: Rejecting class labels shows the group was aiming at a leadership election
options.misconception: assumes electoral aims from label choice

options.text: Rejecting class labels shows the group lacked any coherent theory of change
options.misconception: treats label preference as theoretical incoherence

questions.explanation: New social movements build identity around post-material goals such as environment and quality of life, and often reject class framing explicitly. That is a coherent identity choice, not a sign of hidden ideology or incoherence.
questions.hint: Consider what the label signals about values.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Infer the source of leverage from a partial concession
questions.stem: Log, 8 February: the shopkeepers' association had 300 members and the landlord had conceded 3 of 5 demands.

options.text: The concession shows the association's three hundred members frightened the landlord
options.misconception: credits membership size instead of the threat

options.text: The concession suggests the association controlled a service the landlord relied on
The concession shows the landlord had no legal right to refuse the demands
options.misconception: assumes a legal duty to concede

options.text: The concession shows the association had already won every point it raised
options.misconception: reads a partial win as a total victory

questions.explanation: A partial concession of three demands out of five points to a specific dependency the association exploited, not to headcount or legal compulsion. Partial gains are common when the counterparty needs cooperation on one point only.
questions.hint: Look for what the landlord needed from them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the diagnostic stage that precedes mobilisation
questions.stem: Log, 7 November: the campaign's own survey told organisers which demands most members actually wanted.

answer.exemplar: The survey belonged to the diagnostic stage, which precedes mobilisation proper. By establishing which demands had the strongest support, the organisers avoided spending scarce energy on issues that would not mobilise anyone, and could later show decision-makers a mandate with real numbers behind it rather than a single loud voice.

questions.explanation: The survey is a diagnostic step that identifies which demands can mobilise people before resources are committed. It also produces evidence of mandate for later use with decision-makers.
questions.hint: Ask why the survey came before mobilisation.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of unregistered residents in a locality
questions.stem: Log, 5 August: a town of 12,000 residents has 9,600 on the electoral register. How many additional registrations would be needed for full enrolment?
questions.explanation: The gap between residents and registered voters is 12,000 minus 9,600, which equals 2,400 people still to register. Full enrolment means closing that difference, not replacing existing entries.
questions.hint: Subtract registered voters from residents.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a two-step relay in an organisational briefing
questions.stem: Log, 3 March: the local association heard the council's plan from a neighbour who had attended the briefing.

options.text: The council briefed every household directly through printed leaflets
options.misconception: assumes direct briefing of all residents

options.text: The association learned the plan from the council at a formal consultation
options.misconception: invents a formal consultation

options.text: The neighbour was appointed by the council to inform the association
options.misconception: treats a neighbour as an official envoy

options.text: The plan travelled neighbour to association, which is the two-step pattern

questions.explanation: Information reaching an association through a neighbour who attended a briefing is the two-step flow in miniature. No direct briefing of households and no formal appointment is required for the relay to work.
questions.hint: Notice the relay between resident and association.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify gatekeeping in the campaign stage of an election
questions.stem: Log, 9 September: three of five hopeful candidates in the ward were told they could not use the party's leaflet.

options.text: Blocking the leaflet shows the party was enforcing limits on campaign spending
options.misconception: invents a spending rule for a leaflet restriction

options.text: Blocking the leaflet shows the ward party had lost control of its own selections
options.misconception: infers organisational collapse from a restriction

options.text: Blocking the leaflet shows gatekeeping at work in the campaign stage
Blocking the leaflet shows the hopeful candidates had all left the movement
options.misconception: assumes exclusion means members left

questions.explanation: Gatekeeping operates at several stages, and restricting campaign resources to endorsed candidates is a clear example. It limits how visible rival claimants can become without necessarily excluding them from the movement.
questions.hint: Ask who controlled the leaflet's distribution.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain absorption into an institution after a campaign victory
questions.stem: Log, 10 May: the movement's two main organisers both took paid posts in the new unit the campaign had created.

options.text: Their new jobs show the campaign had been a vehicle for personal careers
options.misconception: reads a career move as evidence of bad faith

options.text: Their new jobs show absorption into the institution the campaign had built
Their new jobs show the campaign was never more than a temporary stunt
options.misconception: dismisses the campaign's institutional results

options.text: Their new jobs show the new unit has no need for outside volunteers
options.misconception: infers a staffing policy from two appointments

questions.explanation: A common pattern after a successful campaign is absorption: organisers move into the agency they created, and activity falls because the goal is now institutionally owned. That is not evidence of personal motives or a temporary stunt.
questions.hint: Ask where the goal now sits.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare two participation reforms by the barrier each removes
questions.stem: Log, 27 January: the committee compared two proposals for bringing more students to the polls.

answer.exemplar: The two proposals target different barriers, so the choice depends on which one binds. Campus registration addresses students who never appear at the town hall, while a transport subsidy addresses students whose nearest station is too far away to reach. Whichever is chosen should be assessed by the additional first-time voters it brings.

questions.explanation: Each proposal removes a different barrier, so the committee should identify which barrier actually binds before choosing. Assessment should track additional first-time voters rather than total registrations.
questions.hint: Identify which barrier actually binds.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the registered share of meeting attendees
questions.stem: Log, 23 June: at the public meeting 320 people attended, of whom 140 were on the electoral register. What percentage of attendees were registered voters?
questions.explanation: One hundred forty out of three hundred twenty is 0.4375, so 43.75 per cent of attendees were registered. The remainder were present but not eligible, which is the selection effect in visible participation.
questions.hint: Divide registered attendees by all attendees.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a cohort effect from a change in turnout over time
questions.stem: Log, 14 May: in 1995 the youngest group voted at 41 per cent; in 2025 the group that is now youngest voted at 63 per cent.

options.text: Turnout rose for everyone, so the change is a period effect on the whole electorate
options.misconception: generalises a cohort shift into a period effect

options.text: Turnout rose for the youngest, so young voters always turn out at the higher rate
options.misconception: assumes a permanent age ranking

options.text: Turnout rose by 22 points, so the reform of 2005 caused the increase
options.misconception: invents a reform to explain the rise

options.text: The group that aged with the data shows a cohort effect of 22 points

questions.explanation: The same life stage shows a 22 point rise across thirty years, which is a cohort effect because those voters carry different formative experiences. A period explanation would require the change to affect every age group equally.
questions.hint: Track one group as it moves through life.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain informal organisation in a new social movement
questions.stem: Log, 2 April: the group that campaigned for local food markets had no paid officers and met in a library cafe.

options.text: Meeting in a library shows the group was too poor to rent a hall
options.misconception: infers poverty from the meeting place

options.text: Having no officers shows the campaign was never properly organised
options.misconception: equates informality with disorganisation

options.text: Informal organisation fits new social movements built around autonomy
Having no officers shows the group depended on a single charismatic leader
options.misconception: confuses informality with strong leadership

questions.explanation: New social movements often reject formal hierarchy and paid posts to emphasise autonomy and participation. Meeting in a cafe without officers is a sign of that structure, not of poverty or disorganisation.
questions.hint: Consider what informality signals about structure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify preparation as a source of bargaining leverage
questions.stem: Log, 17 October: the parents' group knew exactly which two council votes it needed and which officials cared about them.

options.text: Knowing the decisive votes and the officials' interests is the essence of leverage
Knowing these details shows the group had more members than its opponents
options.misconception: confuses information with numbers

options.text: Knowing these details proves the group had paid a well-connected adviser
options.misconception: assumes paid advice explains preparation

options.text: Knowing these details shows the group's support was already guaranteed
options.misconception: assumes information guarantees a vote

questions.explanation: Leverage comes from identifying the decision point and the interests of those who control it, so preparation matters more than headcount. Knowledge of decisive votes raises the chance of influence but guarantees nothing.
questions.hint: Consider what the group knew that others did not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a supporter database matters across campaign stages
questions.stem: Log, 6 September: the campaign's database of 5,000 supporters became the resource that funded the legal challenge.

answer.exemplar: The database shows why a campaign maintains a membership list beyond any single demonstration. Names and contact details let organisers sustain pressure between visible events, fundraise, brief the press and, as here, support a legal challenge. The infrastructure is what allows a sequence of stages to be linked rather than restarted each time.

questions.explanation: A supporter database lets the campaign maintain pressure between visible events and supply the evidence and money later stages need. It links stages rather than restarting the campaign each time.
questions.hint: Ask what the list made possible later.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the register size after lowering the voting age
questions.stem: Log, 12 December: a county's register held 420,000 names before a reform lowered the voting age and added 15,000 electors. What is the new registered total?
questions.explanation: Lowering the voting age adds electors without displacing anyone, so 420,000 plus 15,000 equals 435,000 registered voters. Age-based enlargement is purely additive to the register.
questions.hint: Add the newly eligible electors.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a policy decision reached residents without a newsletter

stimulus.body: A resident asked why the park gate stays locked after dark. The councillor explained that the closure had been decided months earlier and reported through the local newsletter, which residents said they rarely read.

questions.stem: Which reading best describes how the closure decision reached most residents?

options.text: The decision reached residents directly through the newsletter
options.misconception: treats a low-readership notice as mass contact

options.text: The decision never reached residents at all because the gate stayed locked
options.misconception: infers non-communication from the outcome

options.text: Personal contact carried the decision where the newsletter failed
The councillor consulted every resident before taking the decision
options.misconception: invents a consultation that did not occur

questions.explanation: Residents learned of the closure by asking the councillor personally after the newsletter failed, which is a relay through an opinion-holder rather than direct mass contact. The decision itself was made months earlier.
questions.hint: Consider the channel that actually worked.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a structural gate on candidate access
questions.stem: Log, 19 January: the party's membership rules required a long period in the branch before anyone could stand.

options.text: The rule shows the party fears electoral defeat and wants only loyalists
options.misconception: infers fear from a membership rule

options.text: The rule shows the party has abandoned the idea of open selection
options.misconception: overstates a rule as abandonment of selection

options.text: The rule shows the branch cannot afford to train new candidates properly
options.misconception: explains a rule by cost, which the log omits

options.text: The rule is a structural gate that filters who can reach a candidacy

questions.explanation: A period in the branch before standing is a structural gate because it filters the candidate pool before selection begins. Such rules shape access to candidacy, whatever the motives behind them.
questions.hint: Ask which candidates the rule excludes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain differing turnout at celebration and working group meetings
questions.stem: Log, 30 July: the campaign's victory party drew 400 people, but the working groups that followed drew a dozen.

options.text: The weak working groups show the campaign had no real internal organisation
options.misconception: judges the victory event as the organisation

options.text: The gap shows attention turns from celebration to routine administration
The weak working groups show the party's success was not genuinely popular
options.misconception: infers fake support from attendance at a meeting

options.text: The weak working groups show the party should have organised more events
options.misconception: prescribes more events instead of reading the pattern

questions.explanation: Public events sustain attention while administrative groups do the slow work of implementing a win, so a large gap between them is normal. It says nothing about the campaign's internal organisation or the genuineness of support.
questions.hint: Distinguish celebration from implementation.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to test a registration deadline change
questions.stem: Log, 3 November: I compared turnout before and after the council moved the registration deadline forward by a month.

answer.exemplar: Moving the deadline changes when the register closes, not who may register, so the comparison must hold the electorate constant before attributing any turnout change to the new deadline. If the register was the same size in both years and turnout rose, the change may have helped; if the register also grew, the effect is confounded with new registrations.

questions.explanation: A changed deadline alters the opportunity to register, so turnout and register size must be examined together. Without holding the electorate constant, any rise could simply reflect new registrations.
questions.hint: Hold the electorate constant before judging.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the registered share of consultation responses
questions.stem: Log, 8 August: a consultation drew 800 responses, of which 500 were from registered voters. What percentage of responses came from registered voters?
questions.explanation: Five hundred out of eight hundred is 0.625, so 62.5 per cent of responses came from registered voters. Visible participation tends to over-represent the electorate, which this share reveals.
questions.hint: Divide registered respondents by all responses.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain a turnout change confined to the youngest group
questions.stem: Log, 20 April: turnout among voters aged eighteen to twenty-nine rose from 38 to 61 per cent over twenty years, while older groups barely moved.

options.text: The rise reflects a period effect, since every group voted more over twenty years
options.misconception: ignores that older groups barely moved

options.text: The rise reflects a general improvement in turnout across all age groups
options.misconception: generalises from the youngest group only

options.text: The rise is consistent with a cohort effect among the youngest voters
The rise shows that the oldest voters were finally persuaded to join in
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the observed change

questions.explanation: A change confined to the youngest group over time points to a cohort effect among them, because their formative experiences differ from those of older groups. A period effect would lift every group, and older groups barely moved.
questions.hint: Notice which groups changed and which did not.
